proposal.hypothesis: The organizers' FM baseline, ported to the DataAPI. The incumbent every candidate is measured against.

node.change_summary: Replaced pointwise logloss training with a within-user listwise softmax cross-entropy (target = normalized label mass per group), same FM architecture/features/optimizer otherwise.

proposal.hypothesis: The FM baseline is trained with pointwise logloss, which optimizes each impression's absolute calibrated probability independently — but the metric only ever compares scores *within* a user's group, and any monotone shift that is common to a whole group cancels out of both GAUC and nDCG@5 (exactly the mechanism the ledger already confirmed for user-side constants). Pointwise logloss spends most of its gradient budget getting absolute probabilities right across users, which the ranking metric never rewards. Replacing it with a per-user listwise softmax cross-entropy (target = label mass, i.e. `y_i / sum(y)` inside each user's group, softmax over the group's raw scores) puts every gradient step directly on the within-group ordering that GAUC/nDCG@5 actually score, using the exact same FM scoring function and features. This is a pure loss change (organizers' axis 1, rated most likely to help) with no new features or parameters, so any improvement is attributable to the objective-metric mismatch closing, not to capacity or leakage. I expect a modest but real gain, mainly on nDCG@5 since the loss is now literally optimizing a softmax proxy for top-of-list mass; I predict primary +0.006.
proposal.grounding: within_user_variance (ranking is scored strictly inside a user's group, so any loss term that only moves group-constant calibration is wasted; a listwise loss over exactly the impression group removes that waste)

node.change_summary: After training the baseline FM, build a per-user "liked-item profile" = mean FM video-embedding over that user's train impressions with long_view=1, then add a candidate-dependent score = dot(profile(u), V[video]) as a second feature, blended with the FM logit via a tiny 2-feature logistic regression fit on train.

proposal.hypothesis: The FM baseline scores every (user,video) pair through a single static user embedding, so a user's history only enters via that one learned vector — it never expresses "this candidate resembles what I actually liked before," a signal that varies *by candidate* and therefore is not cancelled by within-user normalization (unlike pure user-side bias, which the ledger already proved contributes exactly zero). The measured history depth (median 31, mean 43.5 impressions per user in train) is enough to build a per-user "liked-item profile": the mean FM item-embedding of videos that user long-viewed in train. Scoring a candidate by its dot-product with that profile is a lightweight target-attention/SVD++-style sequence signal — it varies within a user's impression group because different candidate videos have different embeddings, so the dot product differs row to row, unlike a user-only bias term. I predict this adds real but modest lift, mostly to nDCG@5 for users with informative history, and roughly zero for users with no positives in train (~5.1%) or unseen users (~1.6-3.6%), whose profile vector is zero and who fall back to the plain FM score. Net predicted primary delta: +0.0035.
proposal.grounding: train_history_per_user (median 31, mean 43.5 impressions/user; enough history to build a liked-item profile) and within_user_variance (a feature only matters through the fraction of within-user variance it creates; dot(profile, candidate_embedding) varies row-to-row within a group, unlike a static user bias)

node.change_summary: Replaced pointwise logistic FM training with a pairwise BPR loss sampled from each user's (positive, negative) impression pairs, so gradient to group-constant terms (bias, user first-order weight) is analytically zero and all capacity goes to item-interacting terms that actually determine within-user order.

proposal.hypothesis: The baseline trains with pointwise logistic loss, whose per-row gradient sigmoid(z)-y is driven by absolute label frequency and therefore feeds the bias `b` and the first-order weight `W[user_id]` — both of which are constant inside a user's impression group and provably cancel out of within-user ranking (already confirmed exactly by the user_side_first_order_terms dead end). Every gradient step spends part of its Adam budget calibrating this discarded component instead of sharpening the cross terms (`user_id × item-side`) that actually move rank order. GAUC is literally Mann-Whitney pairwise AUC, so replacing the pointwise loss with a **pairwise BPR loss sampled within each user's positive/negative pairs** should align training directly with what is scored: for a pair (i,j) from the same user, the loss depends only on z_i − z_j, so any term shared identically by i and j (the global bias b, and — critically — the user's own first-order weight/embedding contribution that doesn't interact with the item side) receives *exactly zero gradient by construction*, algebraically forcing all learning capacity into the item-varying interaction terms. This differs mechanistically from the already-discarded listwise softmax (which normalizes over a whole variable-size group and can suffer high-variance gradients on the large fraction of small/skewed groups); BPR's pairwise formulation is simpler, lower-variance, and matches GAUC's own pairwise definition term-for-term, so I expect it to recover most of what listwise lost and add a genuine, mechanism-explainable gain on top of the pointwise baseline.
proposal.grounding: within_user_variance / user_side_first_order_terms (constant-in-group terms provably cancel; GAUC's own definition is pairwise Mann-Whitney U, which BPR directly targets)

node.change_summary: Added a shared-embedding auxiliary is_click head (train-only target, λ=0.3) to the FM baseline; inference still scores from the main long_view head only.

proposal.hypothesis: The "current best" script is literally the untouched FM baseline; its reported 0.6019 vs the baseline's own quoted 0.6016 is a ~0.0003 difference, well inside the measured ~0.0008 seed noise floor, so no real gain has been established yet in this run — the ledger's two attempted changes (listwise softmax, SVD++ sequence target) both regressed. The organizers' profile shows `is_click` has a 0.76 correlation with `long_view` and is legitimately train-only (never usable as an inference feature, per the DataAPI firewall), and click events are far denser than long_view positives, so an auxiliary click head sharing the FM's second-order embeddings should supply a denser gradient signal to the sparsest embeddings (author_id, video_id, duration bucket) than the 33.7% positive long_view label alone provides, without touching inference-time inputs. I add a second linear read-out head trained on `is_click` (train-only) that shares the interaction embeddings V with the main long_view head but keeps separate first-order weights and bias, down-weighted (λ=0.3) so it regularizes rather than overwrites the primary task. Because both heads use the *same* item-side embeddings that participate in the user×item interaction term, the extra supervision can only act through those crosses — exactly the channel dead-end #3 showed is the only one that reaches within-user ordering — so the mechanism is consistent with what's already been measured, not a hope that more capacity or more static features will help (both measured dead ends).

node.change_summary: Added a train-only auxiliary linear+scaled-interaction regression head predicting a clipped log watch-fraction surrogate from the same shared FM embedding table, jointly optimized with the main BCE loss via Adam; inference uses only the main logit.

proposal.hypothesis: The FM baseline trains on the binary `long_view` label alone, but that label is itself a noisy threshold on `play_time_ms / duration_ms` (measured correlation 0.635) — two impressions that are both "positive" or both "negative" under the binary label can differ hugely in actual engagement, and impressions near the threshold are mislabeled by construction. If I add a second, train-only auxiliary regression head that predicts a continuous watch-fraction surrogate (`log1p(play_time_ms) - log1p(duration_ms)`, clipped) from the *same shared embedding table* as the FM interaction term, the extra gradient signal should denoise and sharpen the item/user embeddings without ever exposing `play_time_ms` as an inference-time feature (the aux head and its target only exist during the training step on the `train` split; scoring uses only the primary logit). Because within-user ranking is scored on the shared embeddings, and GAUC only credits discriminative users (0<pos<n), sharper embeddings should mainly raise GAUC for those users by better separating true engagement levels that the binary label alone blurs, while nDCG@5 should move little or not regress (ties among binary positives don't matter to it). I expect a moderate GAUC-driven gain, primary +0.0035, since this exploits the aux_signal_correlation_with_label.play_time_ms=0.635 signal that is explicitly legitimate as a training target per the profile, and is a genuinely unexplored axis (ledger has no multitask entries).

node.change_summary: Reweighted the pointwise BCE loss by 1/user_group_size (renormalized to mean 1) so every user contributes equally to training gradient, matching nDCG@5's equal per-user averaging instead of the row-count-weighted implicit objective of the baseline.

proposal.hypothesis: The current objective is pointwise BCE averaged over rows, which gives every training row equal weight. Since `train_history_per_user` shows impressions/user ranging from p10=5 to p90=97 (mean 43.5), this implicitly weights the loss by each user's activity level: a 97-impression user contributes ~20x more gradient mass than a 5-impression user. But the evaluation metric does the opposite of that: nDCG@5 averages one score per user regardless of group size, and GAUC (per the frozen `evaluate.py`) weights only by positive count among discriminative users, not by row count. So the objective is over-fitting the ordering preferences of heavy-impression users at the expense of the light-impression users the metric actually weights equally -- a group-size mismatch that is invisible in the loss curve but directly costs ranking quality on the sparse-impression test population (test p50=5, 13.6% of users have <=1 impression). The fix: reweight each training row by 1/(that user's impression count in the training batch), renormalized to preserve the overall gradient scale, so every user contributes equally to the loss the way nDCG@5 scores them equally. This changes only the training weighting scheme, not the model or features, isolating the mechanism cleanly.

node.change_summary: Added a shared-embedding auxiliary head predicting watch_frac=play_time_ms/duration_ms with a one-sided (censored) squared loss for completed plays instead of the previously-tried plain-MSE aux head.

proposal.hypothesis: None of the ledger's positive numbers are trustworthy signals yet: pairwise BPR (+0.0012) and both multitask aux-head variants (-0.0006, +0.0001) are all inside or barely above the measured seed-noise band (~0.0008), and none cleared the +0.002 promotion bar, so I don't believe any of them represent a real effect — they're correctly left INCONCLUSIVE. The one direction the ledger has *not* actually tested with the mechanism the organizers proposed is watch-time modelling: `fm_shared_embedding_watchfraction_aux_head` got +0.0001, which is exactly what you'd expect from training a plain squared-error regression head on a target that is right-censored — squared error penalizes a model for "overshooting" on completed plays even though the true watch intent for those rows is unknown and only bounded below by the observed value, so the aux gradient fights itself on ~most of the positive-correlated mass (`play_time_ms` correlation 0.635 with label) and washes out to noise. I'm changing only the loss shape of that same aux head: a one-sided (Tobit-style) loss that only penalizes under-prediction on censored (watch_frac>=1.0) rows and standard squared error elsewhere, sharing the same embedding table as the main FM. The mechanism for within-user ranking is indirect but real: the aux gradient pushes the *item*-side embeddings for near-complete plays toward higher predicted engagement without the contradictory pull from the censoring artifact, so the shared embeddings should separate high-vs-low engagement items more cleanly than either the plain-MSE aux head or no aux head at all, which should show up specifically in GAUC (item ordering) rather than in nDCG@5.

node.change_summary: Added a 6th categorical field, hour_bucket (hourmin // 100, 24 bins), to the baseline FM alongside user_id/video_id/author_id/tab/dur_bucket, unchanged otherwise.

proposal.hypothesis: The baseline FM uses five fields (user_id, video_id, author_id, tab, dur_bucket) but never uses `hourmin`, even though the measured `within_user_variance` shows hourmin varies inside 97.2% of test users' impression groups (vs. only 51.8% for `tab`, which is already in the model) — i.e. almost every user's logged session spans multiple time-of-day buckets, so a video's time-of-day popularity pattern (diurnal content trends documented in short-video literature: certain content spikes at night/lunch/commute hours) is a signal that can actually move within-user ordering for nearly all users, unlike user-only features which cancel by construction. Adding a `hour_bucket` field (hourmin // 100, 24 categories) to the same FM, crossed via the standard FM interaction term against video_id/author_id, should let the model learn "this video over-indexes at this time of day" and use it to break ties inside sessions that span multiple hours — mechanistically similar to `tab` (which already helps despite covering only half the groups) but reaching a much larger fraction of users. I predict a modest but real gain, roughly +0.003 primary, concentrated in nDCG@5 for multi-impression, multi-hour sessions.
proposal.grounding: within_user_variance.hourmin (0.972 test / 0.959 valid, far above tab's 0.518/0.483)
